claims.why: One line for the program, one for the library it was built against, and the comparison between them. The comparison is the only part of the block that is a statement about .NET rather than about whichever runtime happens to be installed.
The program's own row count is small and stable, but it is printed here next to a number that is neither, so the pair has to be dropped together and the shape is what is left to check.

claims.contains: the library is more than a thousand times the program: True
claims.why: The load bearing claim. A thousand is far below the real ratio, which is over two thousand today, and it is set low so that a future version of the library shedding a few thousand rows does not turn a true statement red.
The two facts on this page that are different for every reader, kept in one place so that nothing else on the page has to be.
One of the four platforms this book supports. Anything else here means the lesson ran somewhere nobody has checked, and the rest of the page is then a claim about a machine rather than about .NET.

A three part version, which is what the runtime reports when it is a release rather than a preview. It matters here because the row counts on this page are what one specific compiler emitted, and a reader who sees different ones needs to know whether they are on something unusual.
